description: Crypto Village focuses on cryptographic protocols, privacy preservation, secure communications, data protection, and surveillance defense.

talks.title: What If We Had TLS for Phone Numbers?
talks.teaser: Explores applying TLS-style cryptographic identity and encryption primitives to telephone networks to mitigate spoofing and call interception.
talks.summary:
In this technical briefing from the DEF CON Safe Mode Crypto & Privacy Village, Twilio developer advocate Kelley Robinson presents "What If We Had TLS for Phone Numbers?", exploring caller ID authentication and cryptographic identity in telecommunications. Opening at 00:00, Kelley analyzes the structural origins of robocall fraud, explaining that the legacy Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN) was designed on implicit trust without origin verification.

At 08:00, she introduces the STIR (Secure Telephone Identity Revisited) and SHAKEN (Signature-based Handling of Asserted information using toKENs) standards, illustrating how public key cryptography, digital certificates, and SIP header signing bring cryptographic verification to phone calls much like TLS secures web traffic.

At 16:00, Kelley breaks down the three tiers of SHAKEN attestation (Full, Partial, and Gateway) and discusses the impact of regulatory mandates such as the federal TRACED Act. Concluding past 22:00, she evaluates the operational hurdles of global carrier adoption, legacy circuit-switched interconnects, and the limitations of cryptographic attestation in combating modern caller spoofing. talks.title: Fear Uncertainty and Doubt
talks.teaser: Examines the weaponization of fear, uncertainty, and doubt in technology policy, cybersecurity debates, and public perception.
talks.summary:
Researcher Zhanna Malekos Smith investigates the legal, societal, and ethical debates surrounding human microchip implants in the Crypto and Privacy Village [00:24]. The talk examines the growing population of individuals adopting subdermal RFID and NFC implants for access control, biometric verification, and contactless payments [05:18].

Smith explores the intersection of biohacking and constitutional privacy law, analyzing whether subdermal transponders trigger the Third-Party Doctrine and how physical property protections under the Fourth Amendment apply to embedded cybernetic devices [09:56]. She reviews legislative efforts by lawmakers proposing preemptive bans on mandatory human chipping, evaluates theological and cultural resistance [20:56], and calls on hardware developers to uphold privacy-by-design principles to prevent personal, financial, and physiological data exposure [14:36, 25:25].

talks.title: How to Store Sensitive Info in 2020?
talks.teaser: Reviews best practices and modern architectural patterns for encrypting and securely storing sensitive data in cloud environments.
talks.summary:
In this cryptographic architecture tutorial from the DEF CON Safe Mode Crypto Village, a security researcher delivers an authoritative guide on modern cryptographic algorithms for protecting sensitive data and credentials at rest. Opening at 00:02, the presenter highlights why legacy hashing algorithms are no longer sufficient to protect sensitive secrets against modern offline attack hardware.

At 11:00, the session examines key derivation functions (KDFs), detailing the internal design of memory-hard functions that force attackers to expend extensive hardware resources during brute-force attempts. At 22:01, the speaker provides an in-depth breakdown of Argon2, contrasting the side-channel resistance of Argon2i with the GPU cracking resistance of Argon2d.

At 33:00, the presentation reviews the processing capabilities of modern GPU password-cracking rigs, concluding at 44:00 with practical implementation guidance on tuning memory size, iteration counts, and thread parallelism to secure enterprise password storage. (AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Fun with FOIA
talks.teaser: Demonstrates how to use Freedom of Information Act requests to uncover government surveillance programs and public agency technology practices.
talks.summary:
Cybersecurity researcher and former intelligence analyst Emily Crose presents a guide to utilizing the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) for technical and investigative research in the Crypto and Privacy Village [00:00]. Crose demystifies the administrative process of submitting public records requests to federal agencies, including the FBI and Department of Homeland Security.

The talk provides practical strategies for crafting precise, legally viable requests that avoid common agency exemptions, excessive processing fees, and bureaucratic delays [07:20]. Crose shares case studies of unearthing historical computer crime investigation dossiers, detailing how FBI record-keeping practices (such as FD-302 interview memos) function and demonstrating how researchers can request declassified case materials while preserving personal privacy [14:42, 22:05, 29:38].

talks.title: STARTTLS is Dangerous
talks.teaser: Hanno Böck reveals critical flaws in STARTTLS implementations across mail servers and clients, demonstrating command injection and credential theft via protocol downgrade attacks.
talks.summary:
The Inherent Fragility of STARTTLS

The STARTTLS mechanism was designed to opportunistically upgrade plaintext application protocols (such as SMTP, IMAP, and POP3) to encrypted TLS sessions, but its design introduces severe architectural risks.

Command Injection in Mail Transfer Agents

Hanno Böck revisits classic protocol flaws—including Wietse Venema's 2011 Postfix vulnerability—showing that command injection across plaintext-to-ciphertext transitions remains pervasive in modern mail servers.

Client-Side Credential Theft

Böck reveals that widespread email clients are equally susceptible to machine-in-the-middle command injection, allowing attackers to hijack authentication sessions and harvest plaintext user credentials.

Abandoning Opportunistic Upgrades

The speaker demonstrates ambiguous and contradictory RFC specifications governing STARTTLS, arguing that the security community must deprecate STARTTLS in favor of strict implicit TLS connections.
